title: When Riemann and Lebesgue aren’t enough
text:
Integration theories can be sorted by the way they treat cancellation. The Lebesgue integral is absolute: a measurable function \(f\) is integrable if and only if \(|f|\) is. This is the integral analogue of absolute convergence of series, and it has the same blind spot. A function whose integral exists only because its positive and negative parts cancel, such as a derivative that oscillates faster and faster, is out of reach, just as a conditionally convergent series is not absolutely convergent. An integral is called non-absolute when \(f\) may be integrable while \(|f|\) is not. The first non-absolute integrals, due to Denjoy (1912) and Perron (1914), integrate every derivative, but they are defined by transfinite induction and by major and minor functions, far from the Riemann sums of elementary calculus.
In 1957, while looking for optimal conditions for the continuous dependence of solutions of ordinary differential equations on parameters, Kurzweil (Kurzweil 1957) found a definition of Riemann type. He kept the Riemann sums and changed only the way the fineness of a tagged division is measured: instead of a single number, the mesh, he used a positive function \(\delta\), called a gauge, so that the allowed size of each piece depends on where it is. Henstock introduced the same idea independently in 1961 (Henstock 1961). For real functions on \([a,b]\), the resulting Kurzweil integral coincides with the Perron integral; it contains the Lebesgue integral and the improper Riemann integral, and \(f\) is Lebesgue integrable if and only if both \(f\) and \(|f|\) are Kurzweil integrable (Gordon 1994).
Show the Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, 7)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")

# the four classes of integrable functions

ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((0.8, 1.4), 5.5, 4.2, boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.4",
                            fill=False, ec=GREEN, lw=3))                                    # Lebesgue
ax.add_patch(Ellipse((5.6, 3.3), 7.0, 4.6, fill=False, ec=BLACK, lw=3))                     # improper Riemann

ax.text(9.55, 6.35, "Kurzweil", color=RED, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", ha="right")
ax.text(1.15, 5.05, "Lebesgue", color=GREEN, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
ax.text(7.85, 3.75, "improper\nRiemann", color=BLACK, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax.text(4.1, 3.4, "Riemann", color=BLUE, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="center")

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 1: Integrable functions on \([0,1]\). Every Riemann integrable function is Lebesgue integrable and improper Riemann integrable, and both of these classes are contained in the Kurzweil integrable functions (for the improper integral, by the Hake-type theorem (Bonotto et al. 2021, Theorem 2.9)).
Kurzweil’s integral was born together with an application. Its sums \(\sum_i\bigl[U(\tau_i,s_i)-U(\tau_i,s_{i-1})\bigr]\) integrate functions of two variables, and with them Kurzweil defined generalized ordinary differential equations. These are integral equations whose solutions may be discontinuous, and they contain classical ODEs, measure differential equations, impulsive equations and dynamic equations on time scales as particular cases (Schwabik 1992; Bonotto et al. 2021).
The objective of this note is to give a brief but precise introduction to the theory of the Kurzweil integral and of generalized ODEs, and to their relation with measure differential equations. We introduce gauges and prove Cousin’s lemma (Lemma 1); define the Kurzweil integral (Definition 3) and prove its basic properties (Theorem 1) and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Theorem 2); define generalized ODEs; and show that measure differential equations are generalized ODEs (Theorem 4).

title: When Riemann and Lebesgue aren’t enough
text:
Gauges and \(\delta\)-fine division
In what follows, we define the concepts of tagged division and a gauge with respect to a compact interval of the real line.

Definition 1 (Tagged division) A tagged division of a compact interval \([a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}\) is a finite collection of point-interval pairs \[
    D = \left\{(\tau_{i},[s_{i-1},s_{i}]) \colon i = 1,2,\dots, |D|\right\},
    \] where \(a = s_{0} \le s_{1} \le \dots \le s_{|D|} = b\) constitutes a partition of \([a,b]\), \(|D|\) denotes the number of subintervals \([s_{i-1}, s_{i}]\), and \(\tau_{i} \in [s_{i-1},s_{i}]\) is a designated tag for the subinterval \([s_{i-1}, s_{i}]\) for each \(i \in \{1,2,\dots, |D|\}\).


Definition 2 A strictly positive function \(\delta \colon [a,b] \to (0, \infty)\) is called a gauge on \([a, b]\). Given a gauge \(\delta\) on \([a, b]\), a tagged division \(D = \left\{(\tau_{i},[s_{i-1},s_{i}]) \colon i = 1,2,\dots,|D|\right\}\) of \([a,b]\) is said to be \(\delta\)-fine if \[
    [s_{i-1},s_{i}] \subset (\tau_{i} - \delta(\tau_{i}), \tau_{i} + \delta(\tau_{i})) \quad \text{for every } i \in \{1,2,\dots, |D|\}.
    \]

Where \(\delta\) is small the division is forced to be fine; where \(\delta\) is large it can be coarse. Figure 2 shows a \(\delta\)-fine division for \(\delta(t)=0.06+0.25\,t\) on \([0,1]\), built greedily from the left.1
1 The animated version builds the same division one pair at a time.

Show the Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

delta = lambda t: 0.06 + 0.25 * t

points, tags, s = [0.0], [], 0.0
while s < 1:
    tags.append(s)
    s = min(1.0, s + 0.9 * delta(s))
    points.append(s)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
ax.plot(t, delta(t), color="#2563eb", label=r"$\delta(t)$")
ax.hlines(0, 0, 1, color="black", lw=1)
ax.vlines(points, -0.012, 0.012, color="black", lw=1)
ax.plot(tags, np.zeros_like(tags), "o", color="#d97706", ms=5, label=r"tags $\tau_i$")
for i, tau in enumerate(tags):
    y = -0.05 - 0.022 * (i % 3)
    ax.hlines(y, tau - delta(tau), tau + delta(tau), color="#16a34a", lw=3, alpha=0.6)
ax.set_xlim(-0.12, 1.12)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.spines[["left", "right", "top"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: A \(\delta\)-fine tagged division of \([0,1]\). Each bar below the axis is the interval \((\tau_i-\delta(\tau_i),\tau_i+\delta(\tau_i))\), which must contain the \(i\)-th subinterval.





The choice of the tags matters: the same partition can give a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division with some tags and not with others.

Example 1 (Not every choice of tags is \(\delta\)-fine) Consider the partition \[
P=\left\{\left[0,\tfrac{1}{3}\right],\left[\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{2}\right],\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]\right\}
\] of \([0,1]\) and the gauge \(\delta\colon[0,1]\to(0,1]\) given by \[
\delta(t)=\begin{cases} t, & 0<t\le 1,\\[2pt] \tfrac{1}{2}, & t=0. \end{cases}
\] The tagged division \[
D=\left\{\left(\tfrac{1}{10},\left[0,\tfrac{1}{3}\right]\right),\ \left(\tfrac{1}{2},\left[\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{2}\right]\right),\ \left(1,\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]\right)\right\}
\] is not \(\delta\)-fine, because \[
\left[0,\tfrac{1}{3}\right]\not\subset\left(\tfrac{1}{10}-\delta\left(\tfrac{1}{10}\right),\ \tfrac{1}{10}+\delta\left(\tfrac{1}{10}\right)\right)=\left(0,\tfrac{1}{5}\right).
\]

The other two pairs of \(D\) are fine: \(\left(\tfrac{1}{2}-\delta(\tfrac{1}{2}),\tfrac{1}{2}+\delta(\tfrac{1}{2})\right)=(0,1)\) contains \(\left[\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{2}\right]\), and \(\left(1-\delta(1),1+\delta(1)\right)=(0,2)\) contains \(\left[\tfrac{1}{2},1\right]\). Only the first tag is a problem. Moving it to \(0\) fixes it, since \(\left(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\supset\left[0,\tfrac{1}{3}\right]\), so the tags \(0,\tfrac{1}{2},1\) give a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division (Figure 3). In fact \(0\) is the only tag that works for a subinterval containing \(0\): for \(\tau>0\) we have \((\tau-\delta(\tau),\tau+\delta(\tau))=(0,2\tau)\), which never contains \(0\). A gauge can force the position of a tag in this way.


Show the Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def delta(t):
    """The gauge of the example: delta(t) = t for 0 < t <= 1, and delta(0) = 1/2."""
    return 0.5 if t == 0 else t


s = [0, 1 / 3, 1 / 2, 1]          # the partition P of [0, 1]
tags_D = [1 / 10, 1 / 2, 1]       # the tags of D (as in the example)
tags_E = [0, 1 / 2, 1]            # the same partition, first tag moved to 0

GREEN, RED, BLUE, ORANGE = "#16a34a", "#dc2626", "#2563eb", "#d97706"
XMIN, XMAX = -0.62, 1.32
TICKS = {0: "0", 1 / 3: r"$\frac{1}{3}$", 1 / 2: r"$\frac{1}{2}$", 1: "1"}
TAG_TEXT = {0: "0", 1 / 10: r"$\frac{1}{10}$", 1 / 2: r"$\frac{1}{2}$", 1: "1"}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7, 6.2), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.1, 1, 1], "hspace": 0.35})

# (a) the gauge: a jump at t = 0
ax = axes[0]
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
ax.plot(t, t, color=BLUE, lw=2)
ax.plot([0], [0], "o", ms=6, mfc="white", mec=BLUE, mew=1.5, zorder=3)   # delta(0) is not 0 ...
ax.plot([0], [0.5], "o", ms=6, color=BLUE, zorder=3)                     # ... it is 1/2
ax.text(0.05, 0.5, r"$\delta(0)=\frac{1}{2}$", color=BLUE, fontsize=11, va="center")   # a single point
ax.text(0.62, 0.36, r"$\delta(t)=t$", color=BLUE, fontsize=11)
ax.plot([0, 1.1], [0, 0], color="black", lw=0.8)     # the gauge is only defined on [0, 1]
ax.set_ylim(-0.08, 1.08)
ax.set_yticks([0, 0.5, 1], ["0", r"$\frac{1}{2}$", "1"])
ax.set_title("the gauge $\\delta$", loc="left", fontsize=11)


def draw(ax, tags, title):
    """The partition on a line; under it, the interval (tau_i - delta(tau_i), tau_i + delta(tau_i)) of each tag."""
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    fine = True
    for i, tau in enumerate(tags):
        u, v, d = s[i], s[i + 1], delta(tau)
        ok = tau - d < u and v < tau + d          # [u, v] inside the open interval (tau - d, tau + d)
        fine &= ok
        col = GREEN if ok else RED
        ax.plot([u, v], [0, 0], color=col, lw=5, solid_capstyle="butt")
        y = -0.42 - 0.3 * i
        lo, hi = max(tau - d, XMIN), min(tau + d, XMAX)
        ax.plot([lo, hi], [y, y], color=col, lw=6, alpha=0.45, solid_capstyle="butt")
        if tau + d > XMAX:                          # the interval goes on beyond the picture
            ax.annotate("", (XMAX + 0.05, y), (XMAX - 0.02, y),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, alpha=0.6))
        ax.plot([tau, tau], [0, y], color=ORANGE, lw=0.8, ls=":")
        ax.plot([tau], [0], "o", color=ORANGE, ms=7, zorder=3)
        ax.text(tau, 0.13, TAG_TEXT[tau], color=ORANGE, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11)
        if not ok:
            ax.text(tau + d + 0.04, y, r"$(0,\frac{1}{5})$ does not contain $[0,\frac{1}{3}]$", color=RED,
                    va="center", fontsize=10.5, bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=1))
    for x in s:
        ax.plot([x, x], [-0.07, 0.07], color="black", lw=1)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.25, 0.55)
    ax.set_yticks([])
    verdict = r"$\delta$-fine" if fine else r"not $\delta$-fine"
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: {verdict}", loc="left", fontsize=11, color=GREEN if fine else RED)


draw(axes[1], tags_D, r"tags $\frac{1}{10},\ \frac{1}{2},\ 1$")
draw(axes[2], tags_E, r"tags $0,\ \frac{1}{2},\ 1$")

for ax in axes:
    ax.spines[["left", "right", "top"]].set_visible(False)
axes[0].spines["left"].set_visible(True)
axes[0].spines["left"].set_position(("data", 0))     # vertical axis at t = 0
for ax in axes[:2]:
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", bottom=False)
axes[2].set_xticks(list(TICKS), list(TICKS.values()))
axes[2].tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=11)
axes[2].set_xlim(XMIN, XMAX + 0.08)
plt.show()








Figure 3: Example 1. Top: the gauge \(\delta\) on \([0,1]\), equal to \(\frac{1}{2}\) at the single point \(t=0\) (filled dot) and to \(t\) for \(0<t\le1\). Middle and bottom: the partition \(P\) with two choices of tags (orange). Each bar is the interval \((\tau_i-\delta(\tau_i),\tau_i+\delta(\tau_i))\), which must contain the \(i\)-th subinterval; an arrow means the interval continues beyond the picture.





The definition would be useless if fine divisions could fail to exist. They cannot:

Lemma 1 (Cousin’s lemma) For every gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\) there exists a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division of \([a,b]\).


Proof. Suppose not. If both halves of \([a,b]\) had \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions, their union would be one for \([a,b]\); hence some half \(I_1\) has none. Repeating the argument gives nested closed intervals \(I_1\supset I_2\supset\cdots\) with \(|I_n|=(b-a)/2^n\), none of which admits a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division. Let \(c\) be the point in \(\bigcap_n I_n\) and choose \(n\) with \((b-a)/2^n<\delta(c)\). Since \(c\in I_n\), we get \(I_n\subset(c-\delta(c),c+\delta(c))\), so \(\{(c,I_n)\}\) is a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division of \(I_n\), a contradiction.

title: When Riemann and Lebesgue aren’t enough
text:
The Kurzweil integral
Let \(X\) be a Banach space.

Definition 3 (Kurzweil integral) A function \(U\colon[a,b]\times[a,b]\to X\) is called Kurzweil integrable over \([a,b]\), if there exists an element \(\mathcal{I}\in X\) such that for each \(\epsilon>0\), there is a gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\) such that \[
    \left\|\sum_{i=1}^{|D|}\left[U(\tau_{i},s_{i})-U(\tau_{i},s_{i-1})\right]-\mathcal{I}\right\| < \varepsilon,
    \] for every \(\delta\)-fine tagged division \(D=\{(\tau_{i},[s_{i-1},s_{i}])\colon i=1,2,\dots,|D|\}\), of \([a,b]\). In this case, \(\mathcal{I}\) is called the Kurzweil integral of \(U\) over \([a,b]\) which will be denoted by \(\int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t)\).

When the Kurzweil integral \(\int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t)\) exists, we define \[
  \int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t) = -\int_{b}^{a}DU(\tau,t) \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{a}^{a}DU(\tau,t) = 0.
\]

Remark 1 (Particular case). In the case where \[
U(\tau, t) = f(\tau)\, g(t), \qquad \tau, t \in [a,b],
\] with \(f \colon [a,b] \to X\) and \(g \colon [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\), in Definition 3, we obtain \[
\sum_{i=1}^{|D|} \bigl[ U(\tau_i, s_i) - U(\tau_i, s_{i-1}) \bigr]
= \sum_{i=1}^{|D|} f(\tau_i)\, \bigl( g(s_i) - g(s_{i-1}) \bigr),
\] where \(D = \{ (\tau_i, [s_{i-1}, s_i]) \colon i = 1,2,\dots,|D| \}\) is a tagged division of \([a,b]\). This shows that \[
\int_a^b DU(\tau, t) = \int_a^b f(t)\, dg(t),
\tag{1}\] that is, the Perron-Stieltjes integral is a particular case of the Kurzweil integral. Moreover, if \(g(s) = s\) for all \(s \in [a,b]\), then the integral in (1) reduces to the usual Perron integral2, represented by \[
\int_a^b DU(\tau, t) = \int_a^b f(t)\, dt.
\]
2 Part II of the animation Kurzweil integral and generalized ODEs shows this remark, with an integrator \(g\) that jumps.

Basic properties
For a tagged division \(D=\{(\tau_i,[s_{i-1},s_i])\colon i=1,2,\dots,|D|\}\) of \([a,b]\) we write \[
S(U,D)=\sum_{i=1}^{|D|}\bigl[U(\tau_i,s_i)-U(\tau_i,s_{i-1})\bigr]
\] for the Kurzweil sum of \(U\) over \(D\). In this notation, Definition 3 asks for \(\|S(U,D)-\mathcal{I}\|<\varepsilon\) for every \(\delta\)-fine tagged division \(D\) of \([a,b]\). The integral has the properties one expects from an integral.

Theorem 1 (Basic properties) Let \(U,V\colon[a,b]\times[a,b]\to X\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\).

Uniqueness. The element \(\mathcal{I}\) in Definition 3, when it exists, is unique.
Linearity. If \(\int_a^b DU(\tau,t)\) and \(\int_a^b DV(\tau,t)\) exist, then \(\int_a^b D[\alpha U+\beta V](\tau,t)\) exists and \[
\int_a^b D[\alpha U+\beta V](\tau,t)=\alpha\int_a^b DU(\tau,t)+\beta\int_a^b DV(\tau,t).
\]
Cauchy criterion. A function \(U\colon [a,b]\times[a,b]\to X\) is Kurzweil integrable over \([a,b]\), if and only if for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\) such that \[
\left\|S(U,D_{1})-S(U,D_{2})\right\| < \varepsilon
\] for every \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions \(D_{1},D_{2}\) of \([a,b]\).
Additivity. If \(c\in(a,b)\) and both \(\int_a^c DU(\tau,t)\) and \(\int_c^b DU(\tau,t)\) exist, then \(\int_a^b DU(\tau,t)\) exists and \[
\int_a^b DU(\tau,t)=\int_a^c DU(\tau,t)+\int_c^b DU(\tau,t).
\]
Integrability on subintervals. If \(\int_a^b DU(\tau,t)\) exists, then \(\int_c^d DU(\tau,t)\) exists for every \([c,d]\subset[a,b]\).



Proof. 

Let \(\mathcal{I}_1\) and \(\mathcal{I}_2\) satisfy Definition 3 and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Take gauges \(\delta_1,\delta_2\) that work for \(\mathcal{I}_1,\mathcal{I}_2\) with \(\varepsilon/2\), and set \(\delta=\min\{\delta_1,\delta_2\}\), again a gauge. By Lemma 1 there is a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division \(D\) of \([a,b]\); it is both \(\delta_1\)-fine and \(\delta_2\)-fine, so \(\|\mathcal{I}_1-\mathcal{I}_2\|\le\|\mathcal{I}_1-S(U,D)\|+\|S(U,D)-\mathcal{I}_2\|<\varepsilon\). As \(\varepsilon\) is arbitrary, \(\mathcal{I}_1=\mathcal{I}_2\).
Let \(D\) be a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division of \([a,b]\) and consider constants \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\). Further, consider the Riemann sums \(S(U,D)\) and \(S(V,D)\) with respect to the functions \(U,V\colon[a,b]\times[a,b]\to X\), respectively. Hence, \[\begin{align*}
S(\alpha U+\beta V, D) &= \sum_{i=1}^{|D|}\left[(\alpha U+\beta V)(\tau_i,t_i)-(\alpha U+\beta V)(\tau_i,t_{i-1})\right]\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{|D|}\left[(\alpha U)(\tau_i,t_i)-(\alpha U)(\tau_i,t_{i-1})\right] + \sum_{i=1}^{|D|}\left[(\beta V)(\tau_i,t_i)-(\beta V)(\tau_i,t_{i-1})\right]\\
&= \alpha S(U,D) + \beta S(V,D).
\end{align*}\] Thus, by an appropriate choice of gauges along with the hypothesis, we get the desire result.
Suppose that \(U\) is Kurzweil integrable on \([a,b]\) and let \(\varepsilon>0\). For \(\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\), there exists a gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\) such that if \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) are \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions, then \[
\left\|S(U,D_{1})-\int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t)\right\| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}
\] and \[
\left\|S(U,D_{2})-\int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t)\right\| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2},
\] yielding \[\begin{align*}
\left\|S(U,D_{1})-S(U,D_{2})\right\| &\leq \left\|S(U,D_{1})-\int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t)\right\| + \left\|S(U,D_{2})-\int_{a}^{b}DU(\tau,t)\right\|\\
& < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2} + \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon.
\end{align*}\]

Conversely, suppose that the Cauchy Criterion holds. For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), taking \(\varepsilon = \dfrac{1}{n}\), there exists a gauge \(\delta_n\) on \([a,b]\) such that \[
\left\|S(U,D_1) - S(U,D_2)\right\| < \frac{1}{n},
\] for all \(\delta_n\)-fine tagged divisions \(D_1, D_2\) of \([a,b]\). Without loss of generality, we may assume that the sequence of gauges is non-increasing, that is, \(\delta_{n+1}(t) \le \delta_n(t)\) for all \(t\in[a,b]\) and \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) (otherwise, we could consider \(\tilde{\delta}_n = \min\limits{1\le k\le n} \delta_k\)).
For each \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), select a \(\delta_n\)-fine tagged division \(D_n\) of \([a,b]\). Since \(\mathbb{R}\) is a vector space, the Riemann sum \(S(U,D_n)\) belongs to \(\mathbb{R}\) for every \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). Moreover, for any \(m \ge n \ge n_0\), since \(\delta_m \le \delta_n\), the division \(D_m\) is also \(\delta_n\)-fine. Thus, applying the Cauchy condition with respect to \(\delta_n\) yields \[
\left\|S(U,D_n) - S(U,D_m)\right\| < \frac{1}{n} \le \frac{1}{n_0}.
\] Consequently, \((S(U,D_n))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\) is a Cauchy sequence in \(\mathbb{R}\). Since \(X\) is complete, this sequence converges to a limit \(B \in X\), that is, \[
    \lim_{n\to\infty} S(U,D_n) = B.
\] It remains to show that \(B\) is indeed the Kurzweil integral of \(U\). Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. By the Archimedean property, choose \(n_0 \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(1/n_0 < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\). Since \(S(U,D_n) \to B\), we can choose \(K \ge n_0\) large enough so that \[
    \left\|S(U,D_K) - B\right\| < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}.
\] Set \(\delta = \delta_K\). For any \(\delta\)-fine tagged division \(D\) of \([a,b]\), since \(D\) and \(D_K\) are both \(\delta_K\)-fine, we obtain \[\begin{align*}
        \left\|S(U,D) - B\right\| &\le \left\|S(U,D) - S(U,D_K)\right\| + \left\|S(U,D_K) - B\right\| \\
        &< \frac{1}{K} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \le \frac{1}{n_0} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon.
    \end{align*}\] This proves that \(U\) is Kurzweil integrable over \([a,b]\) with integral \(B\).

Given \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(\delta_l\) be gauge on \([a,c]\) suhc that \[
\|S(U,D_{l})-\mathcal{I}_{l}\| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\quad \mbox{with}\quad \mathcal{I}_{l} = \int_{a}^{c}DU(\tau,t),
\] for every \(\delta_l\)-fine tagged division of \([a,c]\), and \(\delta_r\) be gauges on \([c,b]\) such that \[
\|S(U,D_{r})-\mathcal{I}_{r}\| < \dfrac{\varepsilon}{2},\quad \mbox{with}\quad \mathcal{I}_{r} = \int_{c}^{b}DU(\tau,t),
\] for every \(\delta_r\)-fine tagged division of \([c,b]\). Consider \(\widetilde{\delta}\) given by \[
\widetilde{\delta}(\tau)=\begin{cases}
\delta_l(\tau), & a\le\tau<c,\\
\min\{\delta_l(c),\delta_r(c)\}, & \tau=c,\\
\delta_r(\tau), & c<\tau\le b,
\end{cases}
\] and define \(\delta\colon[a,b]\to(0,\infty)\) such that \[
\begin{cases}
\delta(\tau) < \min\left\{\widetilde{\delta},\dfrac{|\tau-c|}{2}\right\},& \tau\neq c\\
\delta(c) = \widetilde{\delta}(c),& \mbox{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Let us assume that \(D=\{s_{0},\tau_{1},s_{1},\dots,s_{k-1},\tau_{k},s_{k}\}\) is a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division of \([a,b]\). Then, there exists an index \(m\) such that \(c\in[s_{m-1},s_{m}]\). By construction of the gauge \(\delta\), we must have \(\tau_{m}=c\), i.e., a subinterval that contains \(c\) in its interior is tagged at \(c\), and we may split it at \(c\) without changing the sum: \[
U(c,s_i)-U(c,s_{i-1})=\bigl[U(c,c)-U(c,s_{i-1})\bigr]+\bigl[U(c,s_i)-U(c,c)\bigr].
\] After this split, the pairs lying in \([a,c]\) form a \(\delta_l\)-fine tagged division \(D_l\) of \([a,c]\), those lying in \([c,b]\) form a \(\delta_r\)-fine tagged division \(D_r\) of \([c,b]\), and \[
S(U,D) = S(U,D_l) + S(U,D_r)
\] Therefore \[
\left\|S(U,D)-\int_a^c DU(\tau,t)-\int_c^b DU(\tau,t)\right\| < \varepsilon.
\]

Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and suppose that \(U\) is Kurzweil integrable over \([a,b]\). Hence, Cauchy criterion yields the existence of a gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\) such that \[
\left\|S(U,D_1)-S(U,D_2)\right\| < \varepsilon,
\] for every \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions \(D_{1},D_{2}\) of \([a,b]\). Let \(\widetilde{D}_{1},\widetilde{D}_{2}\) be arbitrary \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions of \([c,d]\), with \(a<c<d<b\). Moreover, by the Cousin’s Lemma, consider \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions \(\widetilde{D}_{l}\) of \([a,c]\) and \(\widetilde{D}_{r}\) of \([d,b]\). Define \(D_{1}=\widetilde{D}_{l}\cup\widetilde{D}_{1}\cup\widetilde{D}_{r}\) and \(D_{2}=\widetilde{D}_{l}\cup\widetilde{D}_{2}\cup\widetilde{D}_{r}\).

By construction, we have that \(D_{1}\) and \(D_{2}\) are \(\delta\)-fine tagged divisions of \([a,b]\) such that \[
\left\|S(U,\widetilde{D}_{1})-S(U,\widetilde{D}_{2})\right\| = \left\|S(U,D_{1})-S(U,D_{2})\right\| < \varepsilon.
\] Hence, using Cauchy criterion one more time, we have the existence of \(\int_{c}^{d}DU(\tau,t)\).



The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says that integration undoes differentiation: if \(F\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at every point of \([a,b]\) and \(f=F'\), then \[
\int_a^b f(t)\,dt=F(b)-F(a).
\] Whether this is a theorem depends on the integral. For the Riemann and the Lebesgue integrals it holds only after a hypothesis on \(f\) is added (Table 1).



Table 1: When does \(\int_a^b F'=F(b)-F(a)\) hold for a function \(F\) differentiable at every point of \([a,b]\)?

The Riemann hypothesis fails in two ways. A derivative may be unbounded, as in Example 2 below, and then a single Riemann sum can be made as large as we like by moving one tag. Even a bounded derivative need not be Riemann integrable: in 1881 Volterra constructed a differentiable function whose derivative is bounded but discontinuous on a set of positive measure. The Lebesgue integral repairs the second failure, since a derivative is measurable, so a bounded derivative lies in \(L^1\). It cannot repair the first one. Being absolute, it integrates \(f\) only if it also integrates \(|f|\), and a derivative can oscillate so fast that \(\int_a^b|f|=\infty\) although \(F(b)-F(a)\) is finite. This is exactly what happens in Example 2.
The Kurzweil integral needs no hypothesis at all: every derivative is Kurzweil integrable, and its integral is the increment of its primitive. The reason is that the definition of the derivative already provides a gauge. For each \(\varepsilon>0\), differentiability of \(F\) at \(\tau\) gives a radius \(\delta(\tau)>0\) such that \(F(t)-F(\tau)-f(\tau)(t-\tau)\) is small compared with \(|t-\tau|\) whenever \(|t-\tau|<\delta(\tau)\). This radius depends on \(\tau\). To run the same argument for the Riemann integral, one would need a single \(\delta\) that works for all \(\tau\) at once, that is, uniform differentiability of \(F\), which holds when \(f\) is continuous but fails in general. Definition 3 accepts \(\tau\mapsto\delta(\tau)\) as it comes, and this is the heart of the proof of Theorem 2. The result even survives countably many bad points: if \(F\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable except at countably many points, then \(F'\), defined arbitrarily at those points, is Kurzweil integrable and the formula above holds (Bonotto et al. 2021, Theorem 1.75).
The price is that the integral is non-absolute. In Example 2, \(f\) is Kurzweil integrable but \(|f|\) is not, since a function \(f\) such that both \(f\) and \(|f|\) are Kurzweil integrable is Lebesgue integrable (Gordon 1994).
In what follows, consider \(X=\mathbb{R}\).

Theorem 2 (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus) Let \(F\colon[a,b]\to \mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at every point of \([a,b]\) (one-sided at \(a\) and \(b\)) and let \(f=F'\). Then \(f\) is Kurzweil integrable over \([a,b]\) and \[
\int_a^b f(t)\,dt=F(b)-F(a).
\tag{2}\]


Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). For each \(\tau\in[a,b]\), the differentiability of \(F\) at \(\tau\) gives \(\delta(\tau)>0\) such that \[
\begin{cases}
\left|F(t)-F(\tau)-f(\tau)(t-\tau)\right| < \varepsilon|t-\tau|\\
\left|F(\tau)-F(s)-f(\tau)(s-\tau)\right| < \varepsilon|\tau-s|
\end{cases}
\tag{3}\] whenever \(\tau-\delta(\tau)<s<\tau<t<\tau+\delta(\tau)\).
This defines a gauge \(\delta\) on \([a,b]\). Note that \(\delta(\tau)\) may depend on \(\tau\) and nothing requires a uniform choice. Let \(D=\{(\tau_i,[s_{i-1},s_i])\}\) be a \(\delta\)-fine tagged division of \([a,b]\). Since \[
\tau_i\in[s_{i-1},s_i]\subset(\tau_i-\delta(\tau_i),\tau_i+\delta(\tau_i)),
\] we may apply (3) with \(\tau=\tau_i\) fixed, once with \(t=s_i\) and once with \(t=s_{i-1}\), which yields the following: \[
\left|f(\tau_i)(s_i-s_{i-1})-\left[F(s_i)-F(s_{i-1})\right]\right| < \varepsilon\,(s_i-s_{i-1}).
\] Here \(f(\tau_i)(s_i-s_{i-1})=U(\tau_i,s_i)-U(\tau_i,s_{i-1})\) for \(U(\tau,t)=f(\tau)\,t\). Summing over \(i\) and using that \(\sum_{i=1}^{|D|}\bigl[F(s_i)-F(s_{i-1})\bigr]=F(b)-F(a)\) telescopes, \[
\left|S(U,D)-\left[F(b)-F(a)\right]\right|\le\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^{|D|}(s_i-s_{i-1}) = \varepsilon\,(b-a)
\] for every \(\delta\)-fine tagged division \(D\) of \([a,b]\). Running the argument with \(\varepsilon/(b-a+1)\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) gives exactly the condition of Definition 3 with \(\mathcal{I}=F(b)-F(a)\).

The next example shows that the hypotheses in the first two rows of Table 1 can genuinely fail, while Theorem 2 still applies.

Example 2 (A derivative that is neither Riemann nor Lebesgue integrable) Let \(F\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) be given by \[
F(t)=\begin{cases} t^{2}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{t^{2}}\right), & 0<t\le 1,\\[4pt] 0, & t=0.\end{cases}
\]
\(F\) is differentiable at every point of \([0,1]\). Hence \[
f(t)=F'(t)=\begin{cases} 2t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{t^{2}}\right)-\dfrac{2\pi}{t}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{t^{2}}\right), & 0<t\le 1,\\[4pt] 0, & t=0.\end{cases}
\]

\(f\) is not Riemann integrable, because it is unbounded: at \(t_k=k^{-1/2}\) we have \[
|f(t_k)|=2\pi\sqrt{k}\to\infty.
\]
\(f\) is not Lebesgue integrable. If it were, then, \(F\) being differentiable at every point with \(F'=f\in L^1[0,1]\), we would have \(F(x)=\int_0^x f\) for all \(x\) (Rudin 1987, chap. 7), so \(F\) would be absolutely continuous and in particular of bounded variation. But at \(t_k=(k+\tfrac{1}{2})^{-1/2}\) we have \(F(t_k)=\dfrac{(-1)^k}{k+\frac{1}{2}}\), so \(\sum_k|F(t_{k+1})-F(t_k)|\ge\sum_k\dfrac{1}{k+\frac{1}{2}}=\infty\).
\(f\) is Kurzweil integrable, by Theorem 2, and \[
\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt=F(1)-F(0)=\sin\pi-0=0.
\]

title: When Riemann and Lebesgue aren’t enough
text:
Generalized ODEs
In what follows, let \(\mathcal{O}\subset X\) be an open set and \(I\subset\mathbb{R}\) a nonempty set. Setting \(\Omega=\mathcal{O}\times I\), we consider a map \(F\colon \Omega \to X\).
A function \(x\colon J\to X\), defined on an interval \(J\subset I\), is called a solution of the generalized ODE \[
        \dfrac{dx}{d\tau} = DF(x,t)
     \tag{4}\] if \((x(t),t)\in \Omega\) for all \(t\in J\) and \[
    x(t) - x(s) = \int_{s}^{t}DF(x(\tau),t), \quad \text{for all } t,s \in J.
    \] where the integral is in the sense of Definition 3, with \(U(\tau,t)=F(x(\tau),t)\).

Remark. The symbolic expression in (4) serves to define the generalized ODE implicitly through its solutions. In this context, the symbol ``\(D\)’’ signifies that integration is understood in the Kurzweil sense, setting \(U(\tau, t) = F(x(\tau), t)\). Consequently, the notation \(\frac{dx}{d\tau}\) does not imply differentiability of the solution.
To illustrate this, Schwabik considered a continuous, nowhere differentiable function \(r \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) and defined \(F \colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) by \(F(x,t) = r(t)\). Then, \(x(t) = r(t)\), \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), is a solution to the generalized ODE \[
\frac{dx}{d\tau} = D[r(t)] = DF(x,t),
\] since \[
\int_{s_1}^{s_2} DF(x(\tau),t) = \int_{s_1}^{s_2} D r(t) = r(s_2) - r(s_1)
\] for all \(s_1, s_2 \in \mathbb{R}\).

Next, we introduce a special class of functions \(F\colon\Omega\to X\), which allows us to establish, in particular, local existence and uniqueness of solutions to the generalized ODE (4), as will become clear in the sequel.

Definition 4 (The class \(\mathcal{F}(\Omega,h)\)) Let \(h\colon I\to \mathbb{R}\) be a nondecreasing function. A map \(F\colon\Omega\to X\) belongs to the class \(\mathcal{F}(\Omega,h)\) if, for all \(x,y\in \mathcal{O}\) and \(s_{1},s_{2}\in I\), \[\begin{align}
            \|F(x,s_{2})-F(x,s_{1})\| &\leq |h(s_{2})-h(s_{1})|, \\
            \|F(x,s_{2})-F(x,s_{1})-F(y,s_{2})+F(y,s_{1})\| &\leq \|x-y\||h(s_{2})-h(s_{1})|.
        \end{align}\]

If \(F\in\mathcal{F}(\Omega,h)\), every solution of \(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\tau}=\mathrm{D}F(x,t)\) on \([a,b]\) satisfies \(\|x(s_2)-x(s_1)\|\le|h(s_2)-h(s_1)|\), so it is of bounded variation and it is continuous wherever \(h\) is (Bonotto et al. 2021, Lemma 4.9).

Theorem 3 (Existence and uniqueness) Assume that \(F\colon\Omega\to X\) belongs to the class \(\mathcal{F}(\Omega,h)\), where \(h\) is also left-continuous. If \((\widetilde{x},t_{0})\in\Omega\) is such that \[
\widetilde{x}{+} = \widetilde{x} +F(\widetilde{x},t_{0}^{+}) - F(\widetilde{x},t_{0})\in\mathcal{O},
\] then there exists a number \(\Delta>0\) such that, on the interval \([t_{0},t_{0}+\Delta]\), there exists a unique solution \(x\colon[t_{0},t_{0}+\Delta]\to \mathcal{O}\) of the generalized ODE (4) for which \(x(t_{0})=\widetilde{x}\).

The condition \(\widetilde{x} + F(\widetilde{x},t_{0}^{+}) - F(\widetilde{x},t_{0}) \in \mathcal{O}\) guarantees that after the jump (at the point of discontinuity), the corresponding solution remains in the open set \(\mathcal{O}\) and can be extended for \(t > t_{0}\). Furthermore, the assumption of left-continuity on \(h\) could be weakened by imposing the condition \[
x + F(x,t^{-}) - F(x,t) \in \mathcal{O}.
\]

title: When Riemann and Lebesgue aren’t enough
section: Measure differential equations as generalized ODEs
text:
Measure differential equations as generalized ODEs
Throughout this section, \(O\subset X\) is open, \(t_0\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\sigma>0\), and \(\tau_0\geq t_0\). Consider an measure differential equation (MDE) whose integral form is given by \[
x(t) = x(\tau_0) + \int_{\tau_0}^{t}f(x(s),s)dg(s),\quad t\geq\tau_0,
\tag{5}\] where \(f\colon O\times[t_{0},t_{0}+\sigma]\to X\) and \(g\colon[t_{0},t_{0}+\sigma]\to\mathbb{R}\) are functions, and the integral on the right-hand side is in the sense of Perron-Stieltjes.
In order to obtain the existence of solution for the MDE (5), we shall assume that \(f\colon O\times[t_{0},t_{0}+\sigma]\to X\) and \(g\colon[t_{0},t_{0}+\sigma]\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies the following conditions (Bonotto et al. 2021, sec. 4.2):
(A1) \(g\) is nondecreasing and left-continuous.
(A2) The Perron–Stieltjes integral \(\int_{s_1}^{s_2} f(x(s),s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s)\) exists for all \(x\in G([t_0,t_0+\sigma],O)\) and all \(s_1,s_2\in[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\).
(A3) There is a function \(M\colon[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to\mathbb{R}\), Perron–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(g\), such that \[
\left\|\int_{s_1}^{s_2} f(x(s),s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s)\right\|\le\int_{s_1}^{s_2} M(s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s)
\] for all \(x\in G([t_0,t_0+\sigma],O)\) and all \(t_0\le s_1\le s_2\le t_0+\sigma\).
(A4) There is a function \(L\colon[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to\mathbb{R}\), Perron–Stieltjes integrable with respect to \(g\), such that \[
\left\|\int_{s_1}^{s_2} \left[f(x(s),s)-f(z(s),s)\right]\,\mathrm{d}g(s)\right\|\le\|x-z\|_\infty\int_{s_1}^{s_2} L(s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s)
\] for all \(x,z\in G([t_0,t_0+\sigma],O)\) and all \(t_0\le s_1\le s_2\le t_0+\sigma\).
The idea now is to use conditions (A1)-(A4) above, to see a MDE as a generalized ODE and with this to obtain the existence and uniqueness of solution to a measure differential equation of the form (5).

Theorem 4 (MDEs are generalized ODEs) Assume functions \(f\) and \(g\) satisfies conditions (A1)–(A4). Fix \(\tau_0\in[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\), and define \(F\colon O\times[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to X\) by \[
F(x,t)=\int_{\tau_0}^{t} f(x,s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s),\qquad (x,t)\in O\times[t_0,t_0+\sigma].
\tag{6}\]
Then, \(F\in\mathcal{F}(\Omega,h)\), where \(h\colon[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to\mathbb{R}\) given by \[
h(t)=\int_{\tau_0}^{t}\left(M(s)+L(s)\right)\,\mathrm{d}g(s)
\] is a nondecreasing function.

The next theorem is the key step: along a regulated function, the Kurzweil integral of \(F\) and the Perron–Stieltjes integral of \(f\) coincide (Bonotto et al. 2021, Theorem 4.13).

Theorem 5 (Kurzweil and Perron–Stieltjes integrals) Assume that \(f\colon O\times[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to X\) satisfies conditions (A2)–(A4), that \(g\colon[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies condition (A1), and let \(F\) be given by (6). If \(x\colon[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\to O\) is a regulated function (in particular, a function of bounded variation), then the Kurzweil integral \(\int_{t_0}^{t_0+\sigma}\mathrm{D}F(x(\tau),t)\) and the Perron–Stieltjes integral \(\int_{t_0}^{t_0+\sigma}f(x(s),s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s)\) both exist, and \[
\int_{t_0}^{t_0+\sigma}\mathrm{D}F(x(\tau),t)=\int_{t_0}^{t_0+\sigma}f(x(s),s)\,\mathrm{d}g(s).
\tag{7}\]

As a consequence, measure differential equations and generalized ODEs have the same solutions (Bonotto et al. 2021, Theorem 4.14).

Theorem 6 (MDEs and generalized ODEs have the same solutions) Assume that \(f\) satisfies conditions (A2)–(A4), that \(g\) satisfies condition (A1), and let \(F\) be given by (6). Then \(x\colon I\to X\) is a solution of the MDE (5) on an interval \(I\subset[t_0,t_0+\sigma]\) if and only if \(x\) is a solution of the generalized ODE \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}\tau}=\mathrm{D}F(x,t)
\] on \(I\).

title: The history of generalized ODEs and non-absolute integration in Brazil
text: This note tells how the theory of generalized ordinary differential equations and of non-absolute integration, born in Prague in 1957, became an active research area in Brazil, around Professor Márcia Federson, Professor Everaldo Bonotto and their collaborators and students. It ends with an interactive family tree of the Brazilian group.

title: The history of generalized ODEs and non-absolute integration in Brazil
section: Prague, 1957: an integral born from differential equations
text:
Prague, 1957: an integral born from differential equations
In 1957, Jaroslav Kurzweil studied the continuous dependence of solutions of ordinary differential equations on a parameter. To describe the limits of sequences of equations \(\dot x=f_k(x,t)\), he introduced generalized ordinary differential equations, and with them a new integral defined by Riemann-type sums with a variable mesh, which he called a generalized Perron integral and which is now called the Kurzweil integral (Kurzweil 1957; Bonotto et al. 2021, chap. 2). Ralph Henstock introduced a similar integral independently in 1961 (Henstock 1961; Bonotto et al. 2021, Foreword).
The theory was developed in Prague, around Kurzweil, by Jiří Jarník, Štefan Schwabik, Milan Tvrdý, Ivo Vrkoč, Dana Fraňková and others, and their results are described in the monographs Generalized Ordinary Differential Equations of Schwabik (Schwabik 1992) and of Kurzweil (Bonotto et al. 2021, Foreword).

The history of generalized ODEs and non-absolute integration in Brazil
text:
The São Carlos school
The Brazilian research group on Functional Differential Equations and Nonabsolute Integration grew at the Instituto de Ciências Matemáticas e de Computação (ICMC-USP), in São Carlos. Many of its doctoral theses, listed in the family tree, apply generalized ODEs to functional differential equations with delays and impulses, to measure functional differential equations and dynamic equations on time scales, and to linear equations in Banach spaces.

title: The history of generalized ODEs and non-absolute integration in Brazil
text:
The 2021 monograph
In 2021, members of the group published Generalized Ordinary Differential Equations in Abstract Spaces and Applications, edited by Everaldo M. Bonotto, Márcia Federson and Jaqueline G. Mesquita, with fourteen contributors and a foreword by Jean Mawhin (Bonotto et al. 2021). The book is dedicated to the memory of Luciene P. Gimenes Arantes and Štefan Schwabik.


Contents

Preliminaries. Regulated functions, functions of bounded \(B\)-variation, and the Kurzweil and Henstock integrals of Banach-space-valued functions.
The Kurzweil integral. Definition and basic properties: Saks–Henstock lemma, Hake-type theorem, change of variables; the Kapitza pendulum.
Measure functional differential equations. Impulsive equations, dynamic equations on time scales, averaging methods.
Generalized ODEs. Fundamental properties; relations with measure differential and measure functional differential equations.
Basic properties of solutions. Local existence and uniqueness, prolongation and maximal solutions.
Linear generalized ODEs. The fundamental operator and variation-of-constants formulas.
Continuous dependence on parameters.
Stability theory. Variational, Lyapunov and regular stability; direct and converse Lyapunov theorems.
Periodicity. Floquet’s theorem and \((\theta,T)\)-periodic solutions.
Averaging principles. Periodic and nonperiodic averaging.
Boundedness of solutions. Lyapunov functionals, with an application to measure differential equations.
Control theory. Controllability and observability.
Dichotomies. Boundedness and dichotomies, with applications to measure and impulsive equations.
Topological dynamics. Semidynamical systems, LaSalle’s invariance principle, recursive properties.
Functional differential equations of neutral type.






Cover of the book (Wiley, 2021).

How the code works

1. Cousin’s lemma as an algorithm
The file starts with plain Python functions that do the mathematics; the Manim code only draws their results. The \(\delta\)-fine division of Section 2 is produced by running the bisection proof of Cousin’s lemma:
def cousin_division(a, b, delta, seed=None, max_depth=40):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) if seed is not None else None
    pending, division, levels, depth = [(a, b)], [], [], 0
    while pending:
        record, nxt = [], []
        for (u, v) in pending:
1            tau = find_tag(u, v, delta, rng)
            if tau is None and depth >= max_depth:
                tau = (u + v) / 2
            if tau is not None:
                record.append(("accept", u, v, tau))
                division.append((tau, u, v))
            else:
2                m = (u + v) / 2
                record.append(("split", u, v, m))
                nxt += [(u, m), (m, v)]
3        levels.append(record)
        pending, depth = nxt, depth + 1
    division.sort(key=lambda r: r[1])
    return division, levels


def is_delta_fine(division, delta):
4    return all(max(tau - u, v - tau) < delta(tau) for (tau, u, v) in division)

1

find_tag tries a few candidate tags in \([u,v]\) (the midpoint and the endpoints, plus a random point when a seed is given) and returns one whose interval \((\tau-\delta(\tau),\tau+\delta(\tau))\) contains \([u,v]\).

2

If no candidate works, the interval is cut in half, exactly as in the proof of the lemma. For the gauge of the video this stops after a few levels; max_depth is only a safety net.

3

levels keeps the history level by level, so that Section 2 can replay the bisection on screen.

4

\([u,v]\subset(\tau-\delta(\tau),\tau+\delta(\tau))\) is the same as \(\max(\tau-u,\,v-\tau)<\delta(\tau)\).




2. Tags that slide along their subintervals
In Section 1 every tag moves back and forth inside its own subinterval. One number, a ValueTracker, drives all the tags, and always_redraw rebuilds the dots each frame:

3. The derivative gives the gauge
Section 5 computes, for the example \(F(t)=t^2\sin(\pi/t^2)\), the largest \(\delta(\tau_0)\) for which the inequality used in the proof of the Fundamental Theorem holds (see the proof in the note):

1            return F_ex(t) - Ft0 - gt0 * (t - tau0)

2        ok = np.abs([err(t) for t in ts]) <= eps_vis * np.abs(ts - tau0) + 1e-15

3        d_vis = float(bad_d[bad_d > 1e-6].min()) if np.any(bad_d > 1e-6) else h

1

The error of the linear approximation at \(\tau_0\): \(F(t)-F(\tau_0)-F'(\tau_0)(t-\tau_0)\).

2

Where the error stays inside the “bow tie” \(\pm\varepsilon|t-\tau_0|\), checked on a fine grid.

3

\(\delta(\tau_0)\) is the distance from \(\tau_0\) to the first point where the inequality fails. It changes with \(\tau_0\), and that is all the Kurzweil–Henstock integral needs.




4. Drawing a function that oscillates infinitely often
\(F'\) oscillates faster and faster as \(t\to0^+\). Equally spaced values of \(t\) would miss most of the oscillations, so the points are equally spaced in the phase \(\pi/t^2\) instead:

As in Part I, the excerpts below are the key parts of the code, each followed by a short explanation.

How the code works

1. An integrator with jumps
The integrator \(g\) is nondecreasing and left-continuous, with two jumps:
T_END = 3.0
JUMPS = [(1.0, 0.9), (2.5, 0.8)]          # (t_k, size of the jump of g at t_k)


def g_fun(t):
    """g(t) = t + sum_k c_k 1_{(t_k, oo)}(t)   (left-continuous)."""
1    return t + sum(c for (tk, c) in JUMPS if t > tk)


def g_plus(t):
    """Right limit g(t+)."""
2    return t + sum(c for (tk, c) in JUMPS if t >= tk)

1

t > tk: at \(t_k\) itself the jump has not happened yet, so \(g\) is left-continuous.

2

t >= tk gives the right limit \(g(t_k^+)\). The helper jump_curve draws a filled dot at \(g(t_k)\) and an open dot at \(g(t_k^+)\).




2. From Perron to Perron–Stieltjes: stretching the axis
In Section 7 the rectangles of the Riemann-type sum are drawn over an axis that is gradually replaced by \(g\):
        lam = ValueTracker(0.0)

        def P(t, right=False):
            gt = g_plus(t) if right else g_fun(t)
1            return (1 - lam.get_value()) * t / T_END + lam.get_value() * gt / gT

1

The horizontal position of the point \(t\). At \(\lambda=0\) the rectangles have widths \(s_i-s_{i-1}\) (the Perron integral); at \(\lambda=1\) they have widths \(g(s_i)-g(s_{i-1})\), and each jump of \(g\) opens a gap of width \(c_k\).


The gap is filled at height \(f(t_k)\), which is the extra term in the exact value used for comparison:
def stieltjes_exact():
    x = np.linspace(0, T_END, 300_001)
    y = np.array([f_ps(t) for t in x])
    trapezoid = getattr(np, "trapezoid", None) or np.trapz
1    return float(trapezoid(y, x)) + sum(c * f_ps(tk) for (tk, c) in JUMPS)

1

For continuous \(f\) and \(g(t)=t+\sum_k c_k\mathbf 1_{(t_k,\infty)}(t)\): \(\int_0^T f\,dg=\int_0^T f(t)\,dt+\sum_k c_k f(t_k)\).




3. Freeze \(x\) at the tag
A generalized ODE uses the Kurzweil–Henstock sum with \(U(\tau,t)=F(x(\tau),t)\). In the code that is one line:
def F_gode(y, t):
    """F(y, t) = int_0^t f(y, s) dg(s)  (closed form)."""
    return (A_COEF / OMEGA * math.sin(OMEGA * t) - B_COEF * y * t
1            + sum(c * f_mde(y, tk) for (tk, c) in JUMPS if t > tk))


def gode_sum(division):
    """Kurzweil-Henstock sum for U(tau, t) = F(x(tau), t)."""
2    return sum(F_gode(x_sol(tau), v) - F_gode(x_sol(tau), u) for (tau, u, v) in division)

1

For \(f(y,s)=A\cos(\omega s)-By\): the integral of the continuous part, plus \(c_k f(y,t_k)\) for each jump \(t_k<t\).

2

On each piece, the value of \(x\) is frozen at the tag, \(y=x(\tau)\), and then the increment of \(t\mapsto F(y,t)\) over \([s_{i-1},s_i]\) is taken. Section 8 adds these increments one at a time (the pink polygon).




4. A gauge that pins the tags at the jumps
def gauge_jumps(eta):
    """delta(tau) = eta, except just to the right of a jump t_k, where delta(tau) < tau - t_k:
    a piece containing t_k must then be tagged at a point <= t_k."""
    def delta(tau):
        d = eta
        for (tk, _) in JUMPS:
            if 0 < tau - tk < eta:
1                d = min(d, 0.9 * (tau - tk))
        return d
    return delta

1

Just to the right of \(t_k\), \(\delta(\tau)<\tau-t_k\), so the interval \((\tau-\delta(\tau),\tau+\delta(\tau))\) cannot reach \(t_k\). This is the same mechanism as in the example of forced tags in the note.




5. The exact solution of the measure differential equation
def x_sol(t, x0=0.0):
    """Left-continuous solution of x(v) - x(0) = int_0^v f(x(s), s) dg(s):
    between jumps x' = f(x, t); at t_k: x(t_k+) = x(t_k) + f(x(t_k), t_k) * c_k."""
    x, s = x0, 0.0
    for (tk, c) in JUMPS:
        if t <= tk:
1            return _flow(x, s, t)
        x = _flow(x, s, tk)
2        x = x + c * f_mde(x, tk)
        s = tk
    return _flow(x, s, t)

1

Between jumps the solution follows the classical ODE \(x'=A\cos(\omega t)-Bx\), solved in closed form by _flow.

2

At a jump of \(g\) the solution jumps by \(f(x(t_k),t_k)\,c_k\): an impulse.


Section 10 follows Chapter 5 of L. G. Silva’s dissertation (UFU, 2024), which is based on the theory of Bonotto, Federson and Mesquita.

title: A δ-fine tagged division

What you see. A gauge \(\delta\) (blue) assigns to each point \(t\in[0,1]\) a radius \(\delta(t)>0\). A pair \((\tau,[s_{i-1},s_i])\) is \(\delta\)-fine when the bar \((\tau-\delta(\tau),\tau+\delta(\tau))\) drawn under the axis covers the whole subinterval. The first attempt (red) fails; then a \(\delta\)-fine division is built one pair at a time. For the mathematics, see the note Gauges, fine divisions and the Kurzweil integral.

How the code works

1. The gauge and a division that is fine by construction
def delta(t: float) -> float:
1    return 0.06 + 0.25 * t


def greedy_fine_division(a=0.0, b=1.0, factor=0.9):
    points, tags = [a], []
    s = a
    while s < b:
2        tags.append(s)
3        s = min(b, s + factor * delta(s))
        points.append(s)
    return points, tags

1

Any strictly positive function is a gauge. This one is small near \(0\), so the division must be finer there.

2

Each subinterval is tagged at its left endpoint, \(\tau_i=s_{i-1}\).

3

Stepping by less than \(\delta(\tau_i)\) guarantees \([s_{i-1},s_i]\subset(\tau_i-\delta(\tau_i),\tau_i+\delta(\tau_i))\). This is a constructive shortcut for this particular \(\delta\); Cousin’s lemma is what guarantees existence for an arbitrary gauge.

title: Plane curves in Differential Geometry
text:
How do we find equations for a curve that is defined by a motion? For the cycloid and its relatives the answer is in the picture: follow the point \(P\) while the circle rolls, project it on the axes, and use that rolling without slipping turns arc length into distance. The construction and the figure and equation numbers follow K. Frensel and J. Delgado, Geometria Analítica II, Aula 3 (IM-UFF).
These curves are also the first examples of the note Introduction to differential geometry: plane curves and initial concepts, which computes their singular points and the length of an arch of the cycloid.
Made with Manim Community v0.22. The excerpts below are the key parts of the code, each followed by a short explanation.

title: Plane curves in Differential Geometry
text:
How the code works

1. Each curve is a function of its parameter
def trochoid(r, R):
1    return lambda t: (r * t - R * math.sin(t), r - R * math.cos(t))


def epicycloid(R, r):
    k = (R + r) / r
2    return lambda th: ((R + r) * math.cos(th) - r * math.cos(k * th), (R + r) * math.sin(th) - r * math.sin(k * th))


def hypocycloid(R, r):
    k = (R - r) / r
3    return lambda th: ((R - r) * math.cos(th) + r * math.cos(k * th), (R - r) * math.sin(th) - r * math.sin(k * th))


def lemniscate(t):
4    return (t / (1 + t**4), t**3 / (1 + t**4))

1

A circle of radius \(r\) rolls on the \(OX\)-axis and \(P\) is at distance \(R\) from its centre: \(x=rt-R\sin t\), \(y=r-R\cos t\). With \(R=r\) this is the cycloid; \(R>r\) gives the prolate and \(R<r\) the curtate cycloid.

2

A circle of radius \(r\) rolls outside a fixed circle \(\Gamma\) of radius \(R\).

3

The same, rolling inside \(\Gamma\).

4

A rational parametrization of Bernoulli’s lemniscate.


Each function returns another function (a lambda), so trochoid(1, 1) is the cycloid and can be passed around, evaluated or drawn.


2. Rolling without slipping, frame by frame

1            return VGroup(circ(ax, (r * tv, r), r, CIRC2, 3), sline(ax, (r * tv, r), (x, y), WHITE, 2.5),

title: Introduction to differential geometry: plane curves and initial concepts
text:
These notes cover the first topics of a course in differential geometry: the local theory of plane curves. We follow do Carmo (do Carmo 2014; 2016, chap. 1), Tenenblat (Tenenblat 2008) and the course notes of Delgado and Frensel (Delgado and Frensel, n.d., chap. 1). The first examples are the curves of the animation Plane curves in Differential Geometry, in which each parametrization is read off the motion of a rolling circle.
I am especially grateful to the professors who taught me differential geometry at different stages of my undergraduate studies: Prof. João Paulo Cerri, who first introduced me to its basic concepts in my first year, back in 2018, and Profa. Eliris Cristina Rizziolli, who taught me the Differential Geometry course in my third year.

title: Introduction to differential geometry: plane curves and initial concepts
text:
Parametrized differentiable curves

Definition 1 (Parametrized differentiable curve) A parametrized differentiable curve in the plane is a map \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\), \(\alpha(t)=(x(t),y(t))\), of class \(C^\infty\) on an open interval \(I\subset\mathbb{R}\). The variable \(t\) is the parameter, the set \(\alpha(I)\subset\mathbb{R}^2\) is the trace of \(\alpha\), and the vector \(\alpha'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t))\) is the tangent vector, or velocity vector, of \(\alpha\) at \(t\).







Figure 1: A parametrized curve \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\). Each parameter \(t\) in the open interval \(I\) is sent to a point \(\alpha(t)\) of the trace \(\alpha(I)\), and the tangent vector \(\alpha'(t)\) is drawn at that point.




Remark 1 (Curves in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)). Definition 1 makes sense word for word for a map \(\alpha=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) of class \(C^\infty\), whose tangent vector is \(\alpha'(t)=(x_1'(t),\dots,x_n'(t))\). For \(n=3\) these are the curves in space (Delgado and Frensel, n.d., chap. 2).

A curve is the map, not its trace. The maps \(\alpha(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)\) and \(\beta(t)=(\cos 2t,\sin 2t)\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), are different curves with the same trace, the unit circle: \(\beta\) runs around it twice as fast. It helps to think of \(t\) as time and of \(\alpha(t)\) as the position of a moving point. The trace records where the point has been; the parametrization also records when, and how fast.

Curves traced by rolling circles
The key observation is that rolling without slipping turns arc length into distance. When a circle of radius \(r\) has turned through an angle \(t\), its point of contact has moved a distance \(rt\) along the line or the circle on which it rolls. In each example below, this observation gives the parametrization; the link after each example opens the part of the animation Plane curves in Differential Geometry that shows it step by step.

Example 1 (The cycloid) A circle of radius \(r>0\) rolls without slipping along the \(x\)-axis, and \(P\) is the point of the circle that starts at the origin. When the circle has turned through the angle \(t\), its center is at \((rt,r)\) and \[
\alpha(t)=(rt-r\sin t,\ r-r\cos t),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\] The trace of \(\alpha\) is the cycloid.


▶ See it in the animation: I. The cycloid, from 0:10.


Example 2 (Trochoids) Let \(P\) be a point rigidly attached to the rolling circle of Example 1, at distance \(R>0\) from its center. Then \[
\alpha(t)=(rt-R\sin t,\ r-R\cos t),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\] For \(R>r\) the trace is a prolate cycloid, which has loops; for \(R=r\) it is the cycloid; for \(R<r\) it is a curtate cycloid.


▶ See it in the animation: II. Trochoids, from 1:10.


Example 3 (Epicycloids) A circle of radius \(r\) rolls without slipping on the outside of a fixed circle \(\Gamma\) of radius \(R\) centered at the origin, and \(P\) is the point of the rolling circle that starts at \((R,0)\). If \(\theta\) is the angle of the center of the rolling circle, the arcs rolled on both circles have the same length, \(R\theta=rt\), and \[
\alpha(\theta)=\Bigl((R+r)\cos\theta-r\cos\bigl(\tfrac{R+r}{r}\theta\bigr),\ (R+r)\sin\theta-r\sin\bigl(\tfrac{R+r}{r}\theta\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad \theta\in\mathbb{R}.
\] For \(r=R\) the trace is the cardioid. When \(R/r=n\) is an integer, the curve closes after one turn of the center, and \(P\) touches \(\Gamma\) exactly \(n\) times.


▶ See it in the animation: III. The epicycloid, from 2:00 (gallery of epicycloids from 2:55).


Example 4 (Hypocycloids) If the circle of radius \(r<R\) rolls on the inside of \(\Gamma\), the same reasoning gives \[
\alpha(\theta)=\Bigl((R-r)\cos\theta+r\cos\bigl(\tfrac{R-r}{r}\theta\bigr),\ (R-r)\sin\theta-r\sin\bigl(\tfrac{R-r}{r}\theta\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad \theta\in\mathbb{R}.
\] For \(R=2r\) the point \(P\) only moves along a diameter of \(\Gamma\), since \(\alpha(\theta)=(R\cos\theta,0)\). For \(R=3r\) the trace is the deltoid, and for \(R=4r\) it is the astroid, \(\alpha(\theta)=(R\cos^3\theta,\ R\sin^3\theta)\).


▶ See it in the animation: IV. The hypocycloid, from 3:25 (galleries from 4:10).


Example 5 (Bernoulli’s lemniscate) Let \[
\alpha(t)=\Bigl(\frac{t}{1+t^4},\ \frac{t^3}{1+t^4}\Bigr),\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\] Since \(x^2+y^2=\dfrac{t^2}{1+t^4}\) and \(xy=\dfrac{t^4}{(1+t^4)^2}\), the trace lies on the curve \((x^2+y^2)^2=xy\), which in polar coordinates reads \(\rho^2=\frac12\sin 2\theta\): a Bernoulli lemniscate. The map \(\alpha\) is injective and passes through the origin only at \(t=0\), but \(\alpha(t)\to(0,0)\) as \(t\to\pm\infty\): the curve comes back as close as we like to one of its points without passing through it again.


▶ See it in the animation: V. Bernoulli’s lemniscate, from 4:55.

title: Introduction to differential geometry: plane curves and initial concepts
text:
Regular curves

Definition 2 (Regular curve) A parametrized differentiable curve \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\) is regular at \(t_0\in I\) if \(\alpha'(t_0)\neq0\), or equivalently, if \(\|\alpha'(t_0)\|\neq0\). We say that \(\alpha\) is regular if it is regular at every \(t\in I\). A parameter \(t\) with \(\alpha'(t)=0\) is a singular point (or singularity) of \(\alpha\).


Remark 2 (Regular curves in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)). Definition 2, and the tangent line below, are the same for curves \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\), with \(\|\cdot\|\) the Euclidean norm of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

At a regular point, \(\alpha\) has a tangent line: the line through \(\alpha(t)\) in the direction of \(\alpha'(t)\) given by \[
r_{t}(u) = \alpha(t) + u \alpha'(t),\quad u\in\mathbb{R},
\] and it is known that \(r_{t}(u)\) is the best linear approximation of \(\alpha\) at \(t\).
The examples above show what can happen at singular points.

Cycloid. \(\alpha'(t)=r(1-\cos t,\ \sin t)\) and \(|\alpha'(t)|=r\sqrt{2-2\cos t}=2r\,\bigl|\sin\tfrac t2\bigr|\). So \(\alpha'(t)=0\) exactly when \(t\in2\pi\mathbb Z\), the instants when \(P\) touches the axis. These are the cusps of the cycloid, and the cycloid is not regular.
Trochoids. \(\alpha'(t)=(r-R\cos t,\ R\sin t)\). If \(\alpha'(t)=0\), then \(\sin t=0\), so \(\cos t=\pm1\) and \(r=\pm R\); since \(r,R>0\), this forces \(R=r\). Hence prolate and curtate cycloids are regular, and among the trochoids only the cycloid has singular points.
Epicycloids and hypocycloids. With \(k=\frac{R\pm r}{r}\), \[
\alpha'(\theta)=(R\pm r)\bigl(-\sin\theta\pm\sin k\theta,\ \cos\theta-\cos k\theta\bigr),
\] with the upper signs for the epicycloid and the lower signs for the hypocycloid. In both cases \(\alpha'(\theta)=0\) if and only if \(\frac Rr\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z\), that is, exactly when \(P\) touches \(\Gamma\). These are the cusps.
Lemniscate. \(\alpha'(t)=\dfrac{\bigl(1-3t^4,\ t^2(3-t^4)\bigr)}{(1+t^4)^2}\). The first coordinate vanishes only if \(t^4=\frac13\), and then the second one does not. So the lemniscate of Example 5 is regular, although near the origin its trace looks like two branches crossing: one is run through at \(t=0\) with tangent vector \((1,0)\), the other is only approached as \(t\to\pm\infty\).

A singular point does not always show in the trace. The curve \(\alpha(t)=(t^3,t^3)\) is not regular at \(t=0\), although its trace is a straight line. The curve \(\alpha(t)=(t^3,t^2)\) is not regular at \(t=0\) either, and its trace has a cusp at the origin (Figure 2).


Show the Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

BLUE, ORANGE, GREY = "#2563eb", "#d97706", "#6b7280"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9.6, 3.3))

# (a) a regular curve, alpha(t) = (t, t^3/2 - t/2), and its tangent line at t0 = 0.9
ax = axes[0]
t = np.linspace(-1.25, 1.35, 300)
ax.plot(t, t**3 / 2 - t / 2, color=BLUE, lw=2)
t0 = 0.9
p = np.array([t0, t0**3 / 2 - t0 / 2])
v = np.array([1.0, 1.5 * t0**2 - 0.5])                  # alpha'(t0)
u = np.linspace(-0.9, 0.75, 2)
ax.plot(p[0] + u * v[0], p[1] + u * v[1], "--", color=GREY, lw=1.2)
ax.annotate("", p + 0.55 * v, p, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=ORANGE, lw=2))
ax.plot(*p, "o", color=ORANGE, ms=6, zorder=3)
ax.text(p[0] + 0.05, p[1] - 0.22, r"$\alpha(t)$", fontsize=11)
ax.text(p[0] + 0.62, p[1] + 0.12, r"$\alpha'(t)$", fontsize=11, color=ORANGE)
ax.text(-0.55, -0.85, r"$r_t$", fontsize=11, color=GREY)
ax.set_title("regular point", fontsize=11)

# (b), (c) singular at t = 0: dots at equally spaced parameters
tk = np.linspace(-1, 1, 21)
for ax, (fx, fy, title) in zip(axes[1:], [(lambda t: t**3, lambda t: t**2, r"$(t^3,\,t^2)$: a cusp"),
                                         (lambda t: t**3, lambda t: t**3, r"$(t^3,\,t^3)$: a line")]):
    t = np.linspace(-1.1, 1.1, 400)
    ax.plot(fx(t), fy(t), color=BLUE, lw=2)
    ax.plot(fx(tk), fy(tk), "o", color=ORANGE, ms=4, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(r"$\alpha'(0)=0$", (0, 0), xytext=(0.3, -0.8), fontsize=10,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=GREY, lw=0.8))
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
    ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for side in ["left", "right", "top", "bottom"]:
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
axes[0].set_xlim(-1.4, 1.6)
axes[0].set_ylim(-1.1, 1.2)
for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.set_xlim(-1.4, 1.4)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 2: Left: at a regular point \(\alpha(t)\) the tangent line \(r_t\) is defined. Middle and right: the curves \((t^3,t^2)\) and \((t^3,t^3)\), with dots at \(t=-1,-0.9,\dots,1\). Near \(t=0\) the dots crowd together, because the speed \(|\alpha'(t)|\) tends to \(0\); the first trace has a cusp at the origin, the second is a straight line.





Regularity rules out cusps and corners at a point that the curve passes through once: near such a point, the trace of a regular curve is the graph of a smooth function.

Proposition 1 (A regular curve is locally a graph) Let \(\alpha=(x,y)\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be regular at \(t_0\). Then there is an open interval \(I_0\ni t_0\) such that \(\alpha\) is injective on \(I_0\) and \(\alpha(I_0)\) is the graph of a \(C^\infty\) function: of the form \(y=g(x)\) if \(x'(t_0)\neq0\), and of the form \(x=g(y)\) if \(y'(t_0)\neq0\).


Remark 3 (In \(\mathbb{R}^n\)). If \(\alpha=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is regular at \(t_0\), then \(x_j'(t_0)\neq0\) for some \(j\), and the same proof shows that near \(\alpha(t_0)\) the trace is the graph of a \(C^\infty\) map from an interval of the \(x_j\)-axis to the other \(n-1\) coordinates.

title: Introduction to differential geometry: plane curves and initial concepts
text:
Arc length and reparametrization

Definition 3 (Arc length) Let \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be a parametrized differentiable curve. The length of \(\alpha\) on \([a,b]\subset I\) is \[
\ell(\alpha;a,b)=\int_a^b|\alpha'(t)|\,dt .
\] If \(\alpha\) is regular and \(t_0\in I\), the function \(s(t)=\int_{t_0}^{t}|\alpha'(\xi)|\,d\xi\), \(t\in I\), is the arc length of \(\alpha\) from \(t_0\).


Remark 4 (Arc length in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)). The same formulas define the length and the arc length of a curve \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(|\alpha'(t)|\) the Euclidean norm \(\bigl(x_1'(t)^2+\cdots+x_n'(t)^2\bigr)^{1/2}\).

The definition agrees with intuition: for a curve of class \(C^1\), \(\ell(\alpha;a,b)\) is the limit of the lengths of the polygons inscribed in \(\alpha|_{[a,b]}\), as the mesh of the partition tends to \(0\) (Delgado and Frensel, n.d., chap. 1, Theorem 2.1). The same holds in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (Figure 3).


Show the Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

BLUE, ORANGE = "#2563eb", "#d97706"
x = lambda t: t
y = lambda t: 0.6 * np.sin(1.8 * t)
a, b = 0.0, 3.2

tt = np.linspace(a, b, 4001)
speed = np.sqrt(1 + (1.08 * np.cos(1.8 * tt)) ** 2)       # |alpha'(t)|
length = np.sum((speed[1:] + speed[:-1]) / 2 * np.diff(tt))  # trapezoidal rule

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 2.8))
for ax, n in zip(axes, [3, 6, 12]):
    tk = np.linspace(a, b, n + 1)
    poly = np.sum(np.hypot(np.diff(x(tk)), np.diff(y(tk))))
    ax.plot(x(tt), y(tt), color=BLUE, lw=2)
    ax.plot(x(tk), y(tk), "-o", color=ORANGE, lw=1.4, ms=4)
    ax.set_title(f"{n} segments: length {poly:.3f}", fontsize=10.5)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle(f"length of the curve: {length:.3f}", fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 3: Polygons inscribed in the curve \(\alpha(t)=(t,\,0.6\sin 1.8t)\), \(0\le t\le 3.2\), for partitions of \([0,\,3.2]\) into equal subintervals. As the mesh tends to \(0\), their lengths increase to \(\ell(\alpha;0,3.2)=\int_0^{3.2}|\alpha'(t)|\,dt\).






Example 6 (One arch of the cycloid) By the computation of \(|\alpha'|\) in the section on regular curves, one arch of the cycloid, between two consecutive cusps, has length \[
\int_0^{2\pi}2r\sin\tfrac t2\,dt=\Bigl[-4r\cos\tfrac t2\Bigr]_0^{2\pi}=8r ,
\] four times the diameter of the rolling circle.

Two differentiable curves can have the same trace even if their expressions are different. In fact, a parametized differentiable curve

Definition 4 (Reparametrization) Let \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be a regular curve, \(J\) an open interval and \(h\colon J\to I\) a \(C^\infty\) function with \(h(J)=I\) and \(h'(\tau)\neq0\) for every \(\tau\in J\). The curve \(\beta=\alpha\circ h\colon J\to\mathbb{R}^2\) is a reparametrization of \(\alpha\). It preserves the orientation if \(h'>0\) and reverses it if \(h'<0\).







Figure 4: A reparametrization \(\beta=\alpha\circ h\) of \(\alpha\): the parameter \(\tau\in J\) is first sent by \(h\) to \(t=h(\tau)\in I\), and then by \(\alpha\) to the point \(\alpha(t)=\beta(\tau)\). Both curves have the same trace (compare (Delgado and Frensel, n.d., chap. 1, Fig. 10)).




Remark 5 (In \(\mathbb{R}^n\)). Definition 4, and everything that follows in this section, is the same for regular curves \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^n\).

A reparametrization has the same trace as \(\alpha\), and it is regular, because \(\beta'(\tau)=h'(\tau)\,\alpha'(h(\tau))\neq0\). A regular curve is parametrized by arc length if \(|\alpha'(t)|=1\) for every \(t\in I\); then its length on \([a,b]\) is \(b-a\). Length is a property of the trace and not of the parametrization:

Proposition 2 (Length does not depend on the parametrization) Let \(\beta=\alpha\circ h\colon J\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be a reparametrization of \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\) and let \([c,d]\subset J\). Then \(\ell(\beta;c,d)=\ell\bigl(\alpha;h(c),h(d)\bigr)\) if \(h'>0\), and \(\ell(\beta;c,d)=\ell\bigl(\alpha;h(d),h(c)\bigr)\) if \(h'<0\).


Proof. By the chain rule, \(|\beta'(\tau)|=|h'(\tau)|\,|\alpha'(h(\tau))|\). If \(h'>0\), the substitution \(t=h(\tau)\) gives \[
\ell(\beta;c,d)=\int_c^d|\alpha'(h(\tau))|\,h'(\tau)\,d\tau=\int_{h(c)}^{h(d)}|\alpha'(t)|\,dt=\ell\bigl(\alpha;h(c),h(d)\bigr).
\] If \(h'<0\), then \(|h'|=-h'\), and the same substitution gives \(\ell(\beta;c,d)=\int_{h(d)}^{h(c)}|\alpha'(t)|\,dt\).


Proposition 3 (Parametrization by arc length) Every regular curve has an orientation-preserving reparametrization by arc length.


Proof. Let \(\alpha\colon I\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be regular, fix \(t_0\in I\) and let \(s(t)=\int_{t_0}^{t}|\alpha'(\xi)|\,d\xi\). Since \(\alpha'\) never vanishes, \(|\alpha'|\) is of class \(C^\infty\), so \(s\) is \(C^\infty\) with \(s'(t)=|\alpha'(t)|>0\) by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Hence \(s\) is a strictly increasing \(C^\infty\) function from \(I\) onto the open interval \(J=s(I)\), and by the inverse function theorem its inverse \(h=s^{-1}\colon J\to I\) is \(C^\infty\), with \(h'(\sigma)=1/|\alpha'(h(\sigma))|>0\). The curve \(\beta=\alpha\circ h\) satisfies \[
|\beta'(\sigma)|=h'(\sigma)\,|\alpha'(h(\sigma))|=1\qquad\text{for every }\sigma\in J .
\]


Remark 6 (Arc length in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): the helix). Proposition 2 and Proposition 3 hold, with the same proofs, for regular curves in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For example, the circular helix \(\alpha(t)=(a\cos t,\ a\sin t,\ bt)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), with \(a>0\) and \(b\neq0\), has constant speed \(|\alpha'(t)|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=:c\). So \(s(t)=ct\), and \(\beta(s)=\bigl(a\cos\frac sc,\ a\sin\frac sc,\ \frac{bs}{c}\bigr)\) is its reparametrization by arc length.

For the circle \(\alpha(t)=(r\cos t,r\sin t)\) we have \(|\alpha'|=r\) and \(s(t)=rt\), so \(\beta(\sigma)=\bigl(r\cos\frac{\sigma}{r},\,r\sin\frac{\sigma}{r}\bigr)\). In general \(s^{-1}\) has no closed form; for an ellipse, for instance, \(s\) is an elliptic integral. Arc length is nevertheless the natural parameter for the theory, because it does not change under reparametrization: if \(\beta=\alpha\circ h\) with \(h'>0\), the arc lengths of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) differ only by a constant.

Example 7 (The logarithmic spiral) Let \(\alpha(t)=(e^t\cos t,\ e^t\sin t)\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\). Then \(\alpha'(t)=e^t(\cos t-\sin t,\ \sin t+\cos t)\) and \(|\alpha'(t)|=\sqrt2\,e^t\), so the arc length from \(t_0=0\) is \[
s(t)=\int_0^t\sqrt2\,e^\xi\,d\xi=\sqrt2\,(e^t-1),
\] a bijection from \(\mathbb{R}\) onto \((-\sqrt2,\infty)\) with inverse \(t=\ln\bigl(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt2}\bigr)\). Hence \[
\beta(s)=\Bigl(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt2}\Bigr)\Bigl(\cos\ln\bigl(1+\tfrac{s}{\sqrt2}\bigr),\ \sin\ln\bigl(1+\tfrac{s}{\sqrt2}\bigr)\Bigr),\qquad -\sqrt2<s<\infty,
\] is the reparametrization of \(\alpha\) by arc length (Delgado and Frensel, n.d., chap. 1, Example 2.5). As \(t\to-\infty\) the spiral turns infinitely many times around the origin, yet \(s(t)\to-\sqrt2\): the part of the spiral inside the unit circle has finite length \(\sqrt2\).



Show the Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

BLUE, ORANGE = "#2563eb", "#d97706"
alpha = lambda t: (np.exp(t) * np.cos(t), np.exp(t) * np.sin(t))
beta = lambda s: alpha(np.log(1 + s / np.sqrt(2)))          # arc-length parametrization
s_of = lambda t: np.sqrt(2) * (np.exp(t) - 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.9))
t = np.linspace(-6, 1, 1500)
for ax in axes:
    ax.plot(*alpha(t), color=BLUE, lw=1.8)
    ax.plot(0, 0, "+", color="black", ms=8)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")

tk = np.arange(-2.0, 1.0001, 0.25)                           # equally spaced t
axes[0].plot(*alpha(tk), "o", color=ORANGE, ms=5)
axes[0].set_title(r"$\alpha(t)$, $t=-2,-1.75,\dots,1$", fontsize=11)

sk = np.arange(s_of(-2.0), s_of(1.0) + 1e-9, 0.25)             # equally spaced s
axes[1].plot(*beta(sk), "o", color=ORANGE, ms=5)
axes[1].set_title(r"$\beta(s)$, $s$ in steps of $0.25$", fontsize=11)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 5: The logarithmic spiral of Example 7. Left: the points \(\alpha(t)\) for equally spaced \(t\) get farther apart as the speed \(\sqrt2\,e^t\) grows. Right: the points \(\beta(s)\) for equally spaced \(s\) are equally far apart along the curve.
